head.hi: HOW TO BE A GOOD RADIO ACTOR

div.p: The play in this book has actually been produced on the radio. Possibly you have listened to this one when you tuned in at home. The persons whose voices you heard as you listened, looked just as they did when they left their homes to go to the studio, although they were taking the parts of men and women who lived long ago and who wore costumes very different from the ones we wear today.

The persons whose voices you heard stood close together around the microphone, each one reading from a copy of the play in his hand. Since they could not be seen, they did not act parts as in other plays, but tried to make their voices show how they felt.

When you give these plays you will not need costumes and you will not need scenery, although you can easily arrange a broadcasting studio if you wish. You will not need to memorize your parts; in fact, it will not be like a real radio broadcast if you do so, and, furthermore, you will not want to, since you each have a copy of the book in your hands. All you will need to do is to remember that you are taking the part of a radio actor, that you are to read your speeches very distinctly, and that by your voice you will make your audience understand how you feel. In this way you will have the fun of living through some of the great moments of history.

head.hi: HOW TO FOLLOW DIRECTIONS IN THE PLAY

div.p: There are some directions in this play which may be new to you, but these are necessary, for you are now in a radio broadcasting studio, talking in front of a microphone. The word (in) means that the character is standing close to the microphone, while (off) indicates that he is farther away, so that his voice sounds faint. When the directions (off, coming in) are given, the person speaking is away from the microphone at first but gradually comes closer. The words (mob) or (crowd noise) you will understand mean the sound of many people talking in the distance.

Both the English and the dialect used help make the characters live, so the speeches have been written in the way in which these men and women would talk. This means that sometimes the character may use what seems to you unusual English. The punctuation helps, too, to make the speeches sound like real conversation; for example, you will find that a dash is often used to show that a character is talking very excitedly.

div.head: ANNOUNCER
div.p: We present here the story of the famous Revolutionary hero and martyr, Nathan Hale. For the first scene of our sketch, let us go to General Washington's headquarters in New York City. It is early September of the year 1776. In the Orderly room, outside of General Washington's private office, sits Captain William Hull, a member of the General's staff. Another officer comes through the door, Captain Hull glances toward the newcomer, jumps up, and exclaims—
Nathan Hale! As sure as I'm alive!
William Hull! Well, well, this is a surprise!
And you're a Captain! My congratulations, Nathan.
I might say the same to you, William!
Well, as you see, I'm on the General's staff. I envy you! Knowlton's Rangers, eh? Ah! There you have some chance for adventure! Some chance to distinguish yourself, while I—
Why, what's wrong with a staff appointment? I'd be honored if it were offered to me.
Yes, so was I. That's why I'm here. I was a lieutenant of artillery when General Washington asked me to join his staff. I jumped at the chance—
I wouldn't, again! Why, all I've done for two months is write letters, sit at a desk, answer questions, and run errands! It's no duty for a man who craves action!
Yes, William, you have always been a fire eater.
Well, I eat no fire here, I can tell you. Now will you trade jobs with me?
If General Washington asks me to—I'll do it—though you haven't made it sound like a very attractive job, William.
No use trying to crawl out of it now, William.
But you—you're more used to this sort of thing than I am. You're a schoolmaster—used to books and quills and letter writing.
That's true enough. You never had much love for books—as I remember it you were rather a trial to the dominie back home—by the way, what do you hear from South Coventry?
Not much—almost every man in the town enlisted.
Yes, I keep running across South Coventry men everywhere I go. It's a little town, but it has certainly done its duty well in this war.
If others had done as well, we wouldn't be in such dire straits now!
Things do look pretty black for us.
Have you any idea what the General's next move will be?
No!—and what's more, I don't think he knows. It all depends on General Howe's movements, and what those will be nobody knows.
Is General Washington in his office now?
Yes. Did you come to see him?
I was ordered to report to him.
And here I've been keeping you out here—that shows what a good staff officer I am! I'll announce you at once. [knock]
Sir, Captain Hale of Knowlton's Rangers awaits your pleasure.
Ask him to come in at once, Captain.
Yes, sir. [closer] General Washington will see you now, Captain Hale.
I'll wait out here for you. Come right in here! [door closes]
Captain Hale reports as ordered, sir.
Colonel Knowlton informs me that you and your company have been assigned to cover the North Shore line of Long Island Sound.
Well, Captain Hale, I am seriously in need of exact information which you may be able to secure.
You don't seem daunted by the magnitude of the undertaking.
Well, my boy, no man knows better than I the impossibility of some orders.
I hope, though, that this is not impossible. I have to have the information. The safety of my whole army depends upon it. I must know particularly where General Howe intends to strike next.
If he comes across the East River, we can protect ourselves and keep out of his way. But if he comes across Long Island Sound—do you realize what that may mean to us?
Yes, sir. He can cut off our retreat.
Exactly! So that's what I must know.
I'll find out for you, sir.

Good! Now, Captain, you may go about your task in any way you see fit. I suggest two or three alternatives. First, you may tempt one of the enemy or a Tory who has access to the British lines, with a sum of money. You may draw on me for whatever is necessary.
Or you might make a sally across the Sound, capture a prisoner or two, and secure bits of information.
Or, though I hate to suggest it, you might go yourself in disguise to the British lines, but that should be only in a last desperate effort.
Or if you could get in touch with certain persons on Long Island who have been of service to us before—let's see—there is a shoemaker in Jamaica—what is his name—oh, here it is—Simon Carter.
If you can find any way to get in touch with him—
The password is "Liberty" used twice in your first sentence to him.
I don't know what he can do for you, but he is trustworthy and he may have some information.
Now, Captain, I don't want you to go yourself unless it is absolutely necessary. But I must have General Howe's plans as soon as possible.
Yes, sir. I understand. I'll see that you get them, sir.
Good! I believe you will, Captain. Good day.
No. I'm afraid it's more hazardous than that.
You're lucky! A hazardous job! Say, what I wouldn't give to be in your shoes! What is it? Are you at liberty to tell?
Of course I'll tell you, William. I'm to discover General Howe's plan of action.
I should say you had drawn a hazardous assignment! I'd call it a labor of Hercules!
How are you going about it?
There's only one sure way of doing it.
I'll go myself into the enemy lines.
That may involve serious consequences, Nathan.
I know it, but I think it's my duty.
Listen, Nathan. Let me go instead. It's more in my line.
No, William. The General has assigned me to the duty.
But he didn't order you to act the spy, did he?
And he doesn't expect you to.
He expects me to get Howe's plans.
Look here—if I get permission to leave here, won't you let me go in your place?

Listen to reason! You have a father and mother; you're engaged to be married. If by chance you were captured—well, I hate to think of it. But I'm alone in the world, it wouldn't make any difference what happened to me. Let me go!

It's no use, William. I appreciate your sentiment; but General Washington has given me a duty to perform, and I'd be a poor kind of soldier if I turned it over to anyone else simply because it involved danger.
Let me go with you, at least!
Well, if you can get permission, I'd be glad to have you go part of the way with me—though I must go into the enemy lines alone!
I insist on that! There is added risk in two of us trying to work under disguise.
Oh, very well. Have it your way. When do we start?
I'll get permission to accompany you at once.

div.head: ANNOUNCER
div.p: So early the next morning Hull and Hale started out together. They went into Connecticut and began looking for some means of crossing the Sound to the North Shore of Long Island. When they arrived near Norwalk they heard that an American gunboat was lying offshore. They determined to row out to it as soon as night came.
Our next scene is just after dark. Nathan Hale has put on his disguise, while William Hull has found a rowboat, and now draws up to the shore where Nathan is waiting for him.
It's me, right enough. Come on, climb in.
All right. Hold her there while I get aboard.
Easy, you'll have to jump for it! This is as close as I can come with this old tub.
Steady now! Here I come—all right! I didn't even get my feet wet!
Let me take a good look at your disguise. Hm—brown homespun suit—yes—that's a poor enough fit even for a penniless schoolmaster. And that hat! Yes, it'll disguise you all right.
I hope so. Give me an oar, I'll help you pull to the gunboat.
Here you are. [rattle of oar in oarlock] All ready?
Pull away, [noise of regular rattle of oars in the lock and the swish of water continuing]
Where are you going first, Nathan?
I don't know. I'll have to let circumstances direct me.
Are you going directly to that shoemaker the General referred you to?
No, not directly. I'll see what I can do without any help at first.
You better change your mind and let me go with you.
It's no use, William. I won't change my mind.
Let's pull in a little closer.
All right, pull away. There's no light aboard.
No—there wouldn't be. These waters are alive with British boats.
There! That's close enough! Give 'em a call now!
Ahoy! Look sharp there! Don't come any closer! Who are you, and what do you want?
I want to speak to your Captain.
An officer of the Continental army!
All right, William, as soon as I go aboard, row back to shore, and wait ten days for me. If I've not returned by then, go back and report me as lost.
Now, listen, Nathan! I've come this far with you, let me go—
We've settled all that, William, not once but several times.
I wish to come aboard, sir, with your permission.
Hello, there, your voice sounds familiar. You don't by any chance happen to be Captain Hale?
Yes, indeed. I'm Captain Hale. But you have the advantage of me, sir—
Come aboard, come aboard, Captain. Don't you remember Lieutenant Pond? I was in your regiment at the siege of Boston.
Of course, I do, Pond. I'm glad to hear your voice.
Come aboard, Captain, I'll lower a ladder for you.
Lower the ladder for Captain Hale!
Aye, aye, sir! [gives orders for lowering ladder]
Good-by, William. I'll try to be back in a week.
If by any chance I fail to return, will you see that my uniform and other effects are sent to my family?
Here you are, careful now! Give me your hand and watch yourself—there!
What kind of an outfit do you call that you've got on! I'd never have known you if I hadn't heard your voice.
Because I'm bound for the enemy lines.
What? Not on spy duty, I hope?
Exactly. Will you give me passage to Long Island, and land me in some secluded spot?
You can do it without endangering yourself or your boat?
There'll be no difficulty about landing you. There is, however, a British man-of-war, the Halifax, in these waters. We have to watch out for her. But it's dark enough tonight to be perfectly safe.
Good! Can we go at once?
Get the ship under way for Long Island! Bring her into that secluded cove near Huntington! You know the place.
Aye, aye, sir! [calling] All hands on deck! Man the windlass! Weigh anchor! [etc.] [mob, setting sails, etc.]
Well, Captain Hale. This is new business for you, isn't it?
Yes, I've been transferred to Knowlton's Rangers. Our business is to get information. And I am under orders to secure some information that I can get in no other way.
Hm. It's not a sweet business.
It's in my country's service! It seems that you, too, Lieutenant Pond, are in a new business. How long have you been in the navy?
I'm glad I found you here—I might have had some difficulty in convincing a stranger that I was really an officer in the Continental army.
That's true enough. You look—well—more like a country schoolmaster than anything else.
That's what I hope to pass for.
How long will you be on Long Island?
I shall try to be through my business in a week. I wonder if you would meet me at the same place you are going to leave me—say, a week from tonight?
I'll send a small boat ashore for you, soon after dark a week from tonight.
Oh, sir—we won't even think of that!

div.head: ANNOUNCER
div.p: Our next scene is several days later, at the little shop of the shoemaker, Simon Carter, in Jamaica. Simon is sitting on his stool, hammering away at a half-finished boot, when he hears a knock at his door. [knock]
Come in, come in, the door ain't locked! Come on in!
Is this the shop of Simon Carter, the shoemaker?
Are you at liberty today—at liberty to do a little work for me?

lg.l: Now—sir—I'll do what I can fer ye—in the cause of liberty. What is it?
Have you any information for the General?

div.p: Can you give it to me?
Jest a minute. Don't them boots of yours need new soles?
Why, I don't know. I think they'll do.
Never! Ye must have new soles!
The sole is split—the notes are inside it!
Slickest thing ye ever see. And it's my own idea!
I wonder if you could hide some notes I've gathered in the same way?
O' course I could. I'll resole both boots. Give me yer notes.
Pshaw, now—what kind o' writin' is this?
It's Latin. I thought if they were discovered on me—

O' course—no soldier—that is, no redcoat could read that furrin writin'. Well, I'll put it where they'll never find it. Here—right in this sole. Now sit down there and pull yer boots off an' I'll fix 'em up fer ye.
Good! It's an excellent hiding place. Here you are.
Yer a schoolmaster, I take it from the looks o' ye?
That's what I've been passing for.
Now, where's that awl? Oh, here it is. And what name be ye usin' hereabouts?
No, no! 'tis better that ye sit right over there in the dark corner. Ye look innocent enough. Come in!
Good morrow to ye, Lieutenant Drew! I've got yer boots all finished fer ye.
Right! You're hard at work, I see.
Always hard at work, Lieutenant. Here are yer boots. I'll wrap them up fer ye.
Never set eyes on him before.
Unless I'm much mistaken, I've seen him before—but I can't place him.
Eh? Here's yer boots, Lieutenant. An' come around again when ye have need of a good shoemaker.
Thank you. I'm going to speak to him. [louder] Good morning, sir.
Drew—Drew—Lieutenant on His Majesty's gunboat, the Halifax. Are you a stranger hereabouts?
Do you live on the Island?
Ah yes—well, no doubt I've seen you over there. I'm often at Huntington.
Perhaps you know that delightfully charming lady who keeps the tavern—Mrs. Chichester?
Hm! You should know her—a delightful soul. Well, good day—good day, Simon.
Now, where have I met that man?
Then ye have met him? He wasn't mistaken?
I've seen him somewhere—but I can't place him.
Well—as long as he can't place you, yer safe, but git out o' this town as soon as ye can.
Never there in my life, except late at night when I landed on the Island.
Well, I'll git the boots fixed for ye—then git out fast! No use runnin' any risks.
You're right, Simon. I shall take every care not to run into that man again.

div.head: ANNOUNCER
div.p: Our next scene is a few days later. It is evening. Darkness is just falling. Mrs. Chichester, the keeper of the Huntington Tavern, is bustling about her kitchen, when Lieutenant Drew enters the back door.
Good evenin' to ye, Lieutenant Drew. And what are ye doin' comin' into my kitchen, I'd like to know?
Your tavern room's crowded, and I thought perhaps you'd serve me here.
Indeed, I'll do nothing of the kind. There's room enough in the tavern room.
But I'll have no chance to talk to you out there. And I'd as soon not eat as be deprived of your company.
Go along with ye! Come on out here into the tavern room or ye'll not git a bite to eat.
Your word is law—I can only obey.
Close the door, Mrs. Chichester! Did you take particular notice of the man sitting alone in the corner?
The nice-lookin' young feller in the brown suit?
That's the one. Do you know him?
Never set eyes on him before.
He is not! I know every young blood hereabouts. An' he's not a native here, I kin warrant ye that.
What—don't scare a body to death! What have ye got?
I know where I've seen him! He's a rebel.
A rebel! Indeed! In my tavern? I'll go throw him out!

No! No! We must make certain first. But I think he's an officer in the rebel army. Some months ago I was captured near Boston. I escaped later. But while I was a prisoner, I saw this fellow—unless I'm much mistaken. I saw him again the other day in Jamaica, at the shoemaker's; and now—look at him—here through the crack in the door!
He's lookin' fer somethin'—out the winder.
He's watching the shore of the cove!
Lookin' fer a boat to fetch him away, I'll warrant ye!
Exactly! Now, Mrs. Chichester, let's set a trap for him. Will you help me?
I will that! A rebel—and like as not a spy—in my tavern!
Go in to him, engage him in conversation, then look out the window and remark that you see a small boat landing.
If he starts up, I'll know he's my man.
Tell him you're mistaken. The darkness deluded you.
A small boat from my ship, the Halifax, is waiting for me round the point. I'll bring it around with my crew and we'll apprehend him.
Good. Wait here—I'll go in now. [door opens, laughter and talk swell up]
I hope, sir, ye found the roast beef to yer liking.
Can I help ye to anything else, sir?
I'm sorry we have such poor fare, sir, but the times are hard, what with the comin' and goin' of the troops; and the rebels cleaned out the place when they were here.
Oh look—there in the cove! D'ye see a small boat comin' into shore? I wonder what it can be doin' here?
Oh, indeed! I'm afraid I'll have to go, Madam! Let me pay my reckoning.
There—I guess my eyes deceived me. It's not a boat at all.
What was that you said? Your reckoning? But sir, you've had no sweetmeat. Come, sit down, I'll bring ye a bit o' pastry.
I'll take it much amiss if ye refuse me.
Thank you, Madam—I'll wait—bring your sweetmeat.

div.head: ANNOUNCER
div.p: As soon as Hale finished his meal at the tavern, he went to the shore of the cove to await the boat that he expected. After some time he heard the splash of oars. So sure was he that this was his boat that he stood up and called.
Hello, Pond, here I am! Right here!
Stand fast, put your hands up!
What—what's the meaning of this? Sir, I am a peaceable schoolmaster, you have no cause to apprehend me!
We'll soon see. Strike a light! Search him!
Well, sir, I thought I'd seen you before. Now I know I have! I've placed you at last! You are an officer in the rebel army!
I tell you, sir, I am a poor schoolmaster!
We'll soon see. Find anything in his pockets?
Rip his jacket to pieces, look in the lining and the seams!
Why am I suffering this indignity?
Strip him—tear every piece of clothing to pieces!
I trust this is giving you some pleasure.
We're enjoying ourselves, aren't we, boys?
Let's see it—ha—receipt for lodgings. Is that the best you can do?
Perhaps, sir, now that you have ruined my clothes, you'll let me go.
I will not! I'll find where you've hidden your notes if I have to rip your skin off!
I am helpless, sir. But you must be satisfied that I have nothing on me. Can't you conclude your sport and let me go?
Look here, men—what about his boots?
He was having them resoled the other day! Ho, I'll wager that's where they are! Give me your knife, Bos'n!
Hm! There—ah, ha! I thought so! Papers—papers—I thought as much—bring the light nearer! Hm—what's this? Some foreign tongue—Ah! Latin. Who would have expected a rebel to know Latin?
Aye, and a spy as well—as these notes prove.
My Latin is a little rusty, but I can make out the tenor of them. Hm—disposition of troops—probable movements of army—yes, that will do! What have you to say to that, my fine rebel?
You don't need to. We've evidence enough to hang you as it is. Bring him along, men! [mob noise]

div.head: ANNOUNCER
div.p: So Hale was taken aboard the Halifax and delivered late the same night to General Howe, who, without the formality of a trial, turned him over to the Provost Marshal, William Cunningham, for execution the next day.

Our next scene is in the apple orchard of the Beekman estate on Manhattan. Hale has been marched out for his execution. He is standing under guard, near the tent of Captain John Montressor, who, as our scene opens, comes out of his tent, sees Hale, and speaks to him.
Sir, I regret to see such a fine appearing young man in this situation.
You are kind to say so, sir.
May I ask your name and rank?
I am Captain Nathan Hale, of the Colonial army.
May I introduce myself? I am Captain John Montressor. Can I be of any assistance to you?
I should be deeply grateful, sir, if I could write a few lines to friends and relatives before I meet my fate.
Will you come into my tent?
You'll find quills, ink, and paper on my field desk.
I say, halt there—where are you going?
Never mind, Corporal! I'll be responsible for the prisoner.
Very good, Captain, but the Provost Marshal won't like it! I can tell you that.
I'll take all the blame. The Provost Marshal never likes anything, so that's no matter. Here, put this crown in your pocket.
Do you know anything about the prisoner?
No, sir. Ah, sir! Here comes the Provost Marshal!
Where's the prisoner? Guard! Where's the prisoner?
Just at this moment, sir, he is writing a few notes in my tent.
I'll get him, sir, if I may be allowed.
I'm sorry, Captain Hale, but the Marshal is waiting for you—have you finished your letters?
He hasn't finished his letters, sir.
Of course I'll come. May I ask you to deliver these letters at your first opportunity?
Guard, fall in around the prisoner.
Put the prisoner on the ladder!
It isn't necessary, sir—I can climb the ladder.
All right then, get up there. Put the halter around his neck, and blindfold him.
I can do that, too, sir.
All right, then, do it! And if you have any further statement or confession to make, now is the time to do it.
I only regret that I have but one life to lose for my country.
Humph! Now, guard, when I give the word, kick the ladder and let the rebel swing. Are you ready?
Steady—now! [noise of ladder, gasp, etc.] [pause] So let all spies, rebels, and traitors swing! March the guard off!
Poor fellow—and he's hardly more than a boy.
And now, Captain Montressor, I'll trouble you for those letters.
What are you doing, sir? Stop it! Don't tear those letters up!
What did you do that for? They were intrusted to me for delivery.
Well—they won't be delivered! The rebels shall never know they had a man who could die with such firmness!

div.head: ANNOUNCER
div.p: The next day, however, Captain Montressor carried the news to the American lines under a white flag and repeated to Hale's companions those words—which have come down to us: "I only regret that I have but one life to lose for my country!"

div.head: Transcriber's Note:
div.p: Page 28: Corrected both occurrences of CHICHERTER to CHICHESTER.
